hints: Focus on what actually attacks the carbon in bromoethane and what electron behaviour defines that type of reagent.
The attacking $\text{OH}^-$ ion uses a lone pair to form a new bond to carbon, so decide if that makes it electron rich or electron poor.
Remember a leaving group takes the bonding pair of electrons with it as $\text{Br}^-$, so ask yourself what name we give to a species that can donate an electron pair.
walkthrough:
**Write out what happens**

Think of this hydrolysis as a simple substitution. Hydroxide replaces bromine.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{Br}^-$$

**Identify the attacking group**

The carbon attached to Br is slightly positive because Br pulls electrons away. The $\text{OH}^-$ ion has lone pairs and loves positive centres. It donates a pair to form the new C-O bond. A donor of an electron pair is a nucleophile.

**Identify the leaving group**

This is the tricky part. The C-Br bond breaks heterolytically and both bonding electrons go to bromine to give $\text{Br}^-$. $\text{Br}^-$ has full lone pairs and is itself an electron pair donor, so by definition it is also classified as a nucleophile when we describe its nature.

**Put it together**

Attacking group is nucleophilic and leaving group is nucleophilic. That gives nucleophile plus nucleophile.

options.A: Incorrect. Neither species is an electrophile. An electrophile accepts an electron pair, but both $\text{OH}^-$ and $\text{Br}^-$ are electron rich anions that donate pairs.
options.B: Incorrect. It reverses the attacking group. $\text{OH}^-$ donates its lone pair to the electron deficient carbon, so it cannot be an electrophile. It is the classic nucleophile in this hydrolysis.
options.C: Incorrect and the most common trap. Students correctly spot $\text{OH}^-$ as a nucleophile but then call $\text{Br}$ the electrophile because the carbon it leaves is electrophilic. The question asks about the nature of the $\text{Br}^-$ ion itself, which leaves with an electron pair and is electron rich, so it is nucleophilic.
options.D: Correct. $\text{OH}^-$ attacks by donating an electron pair, so it is a nucleophile. $\text{Br}^-$ leaves with the C-Br bonding pair and possesses lone pairs it could donate, so it is also classified as a nucleophile in nature.
